title: How often can migration switch a population above or below its total carrying capacity? Five crossings in three logistic patches, and bounds for any number of patches
shortTitle: Migration can switch a population above and below capacity five times
oneLine: Answering a 2022 question: in the logistic patch model, three patches allow exactly five switches between migration helping and harming total biomass, not three; n patches allow between n + 2 and 2ⁿ − 3. The effects are a few parts per million.
abstract: When habitat patches are linked by migration, the total equilibrium population B can end up above or below the sum S of the patches' carrying capacities: migration can help or harm the population as a whole. As the overall migration intensity β grows, B can switch between these two states several times. In the standard logistic patch model with an arbitrary irreducible, conservative (possibly asymmetric) migration network, Elbetch, Benzekri, Massart and Sari (2022) found three switches with three patches and asked for a proof that three is the maximum, and for bounds with more patches. This candidate answers both. Three is not the maximum: for three patches the exact maximum is five, shown by an explicit rational example with five transverse crossings certified in exact arithmetic and a direct algebraic proof that six are impossible. For n patches there are at most 2ⁿ − 3 crossings unless B is identically S, with no genericity assumption, and for every n ≥ 3 there are networks with at least n + 2; an exact four-patch certificate gives six. So the maximum is 1 for two patches, 5 for three and between 6 and 13 for four. The five-crossing example also has at least three separate peaks of total biomass. The effects are tiny, at most a few parts per million between crossings, and the example needs finely tuned migration rates; the results describe what the model allows, not observations. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Three patches allow exactly five crossings, N(3) = 5: the network r = (7/3, 1, 2), K = (1, 3, 1), Γ = M/138159 crosses S = 5 at β = 46053/252320, 5117/6400, 6579/2912, 6579/1640 and 168861/27680, all transversally, and no three-patch network has six (Theorem 6, proof and exact certificate).

Universal upper bound: with n patches there are at most 2ⁿ − 3 crossings unless B ≡ S, with no genericity assumption; counted with multiplicity, including the zero-migration point, the total is at most 2ⁿ − 2 (Theorem 9, Proposition 10).

Lower bound: adding weakly coupled patches gives at least n + 2 crossings and ⌈(n + 2)/2⌉ strict maxima for every n ≥ 3; an exact four-patch certificate gives six crossings, so 6 ≤ N(4) ≤ 13 (Lemma 11, Theorem 12).
Crossings force peaks: the five-crossing example has at least three strict local maxima of total biomass (Corollary 7).
Why five: the threshold equilibria solve n quadrics with 2ⁿ = 8 projective solutions for three patches; one sits at zero migration and two at a point at infinity, leaving 8 − 1 − 2 = 5.

Effects are tiny: between crossings B differs from S by at most about 3.3 ppm (numerical), with a −249 ppm perfect-mixing limit; one migration rate is about 1/430 of the largest and the example is finely tuned.

narration: Migration can switch a population above and below its carrying capacity five times. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the background: picture a species living in a few habitat patches. Without movement, each patch settles at its carrying capacity, and the total is the sum of those capacities. Now let individuals move between the patches, with every migration rate scaled by one overall intensity. Depending on the patches, migration can leave the total population a little above that sum, meaning migration helps, or a little below it, meaning migration harms. In 2015, Roger Arditi, Claude Lobry and Tewfik Sari showed that with two patches the total can switch from one side to the other only once. In 2022, Bilel Elbetch and colleagues found three switches with three patches, and asked for a proof that three is the most. Now, the main finding: three is not the most. With three patches the exact maximum is five. An explicit example with five switches is checked in exact arithmetic, and six are proved impossible. For any number of patches, n, the number of switches is at most two to the power n, minus three, and at least n plus two can happen. With four patches, an exact example has six. As for how large the effect is: tiny. Between switches the total moves by at most a few parts per million, and the example needs finely tuned migration rates. So this is about what the model allows, not about real populations. As for how sure this is: every theorem has a written proof, and the examples are certified in exact arithmetic. Finally, the limits: review so far is internal and AI-assisted, and the literature search was bounded. This briefing describes version one point zero candidate, released on the thirty-first of October 2026; the paper and evidence are linked from the release page. This audio uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional evidence.
